claim: Suspending processes lets you investigate or troubleshoot without interference from scaling policies or scheduled actions, and stops EC2 Auto Scaling from marking instances unhealthy and replacing them while you change the group.
question: Why would you suspend Auto Scaling processes?

values.display: investigate or troubleshoot an issue without interference
marking instances unhealthy and replacing them

evidence.quote: Suspending processes can be useful when you need to investigate or troubleshoot an issue without interference from scaling policies or scheduled actions. It also helps prevent Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling from marking instances unhealthy and replacing them while you are making changes to your Auto Scaling group.

claim: EC2 Auto Scaling can itself suspend processes (an administrative suspension), most commonly for groups that have tried to launch instances for over 24 hours without launching any; you can resume them.
question: When does EC2 Auto Scaling suspend a group's processes on its own?

evidence.quote: An administrative suspension most commonly applies to Auto Scaling groups that have been trying to launch instances for over 24 hours but have not succeeded in launching any instances. You can resume processes that were suspended by Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling for administrative reasons.

claim: The Launch process adds instances to the group when it scales out or when EC2 Auto Scaling launches instances for other reasons, such as adding instances to a warm pool.
question: What does the Launch process do, so what stops when you suspend it?

values.display: Adds instances to the Auto Scaling group

evidence.quote: `Launch` – Adds instances to the Auto Scaling group when the group scales out, or when Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling chooses to launch instances for other reasons, such as when it adds instances to a warm pool.

claim: The Terminate process removes instances when the group scales in or for other reasons, such as exceeding the maximum instance lifetime or failing a health check.
question: What does the Terminate process cover?

values.display: Removes instances from the Auto Scaling group

evidence.quote: `Terminate` – Removes instances from the Auto Scaling group when the group scales in, or when Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling chooses to terminate instances for other reasons, such as when an instance is terminated for exceeding its maximum lifetime duration or failing a health check.

claim: The HealthCheck process checks instance health and marks an instance unhealthy when Amazon EC2 or Elastic Load Balancing reports it unhealthy; it can override a health status you set manually.
question: What does the HealthCheck process do?

evidence.quote: `HealthCheck` – Checks the health of the instances and marks an instance as unhealthy if Amazon EC2 or Elastic Load Balancing tells Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling that the instance is unhealthy. This process can override the health status of an instance that you set manually.

claim: The ReplaceUnhealthy process terminates instances marked unhealthy and launches new instances to replace them.
question: Which process terminates and replaces unhealthy instances?

values.display: Terminates instances that are marked as unhealthy

evidence.quote: `ReplaceUnhealthy` – Terminates instances that are marked as unhealthy and then creates new instances to replace them.

claim: The AZRebalance process balances the number of instances evenly across the group's Availability Zones when the group becomes unbalanced, for example when an unavailable zone becomes healthy again.
question: Which process evens out instances across Availability Zones?

values.display: Balances the number of EC2 instances

evidence.quote: `AZRebalance` – Balances the number of EC2 instances in the group evenly across all of the specified Availability Zones when the group becomes unbalanced, for example, when a previously unavailable Availability Zone returns to a healthy state.

claim: The AlarmNotification process accepts notifications from the CloudWatch alarms of dynamic scaling policies; suspending it stops those policies from acting.
question: Which process lets CloudWatch alarms trigger dynamic scaling policies?

evidence.quote: `AlarmNotification` – Accepts notifications from CloudWatch alarms that are associated with dynamic scaling policies.

claim: The ScheduledActions process performs scheduled scaling actions, including those created by an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan with predictive scaling turned on.
question: Which process runs scheduled scaling actions?

evidence.quote: `ScheduledActions` – Performs the scheduled scaling actions that you create or that are created for you when you create an AWS Auto Scaling scaling plan and turn on predictive scaling.

claim: The AddToLoadBalancer process adds instances to the attached load balancer target group or Classic Load Balancer when they launch.
question: Which process registers new instances with the attached load balancer?

values.display: Adds instances to the attached load balancer

evidence.quote: `AddToLoadBalancer` – Adds instances to the attached load balancer target group or Classic Load Balancer when they are launched.

claim: The Elastic Load Balancing health check type checks whether the load balancer reports the instance as healthy and able to handle requests; you must turn it on for the group.
question: Does an Auto Scaling group use the load balancer's health checks without extra configuration?

evidence.quote: | Elastic Load Balancing health checks | +  Checks whether the load balancer reports the instance as healthy, confirming whether the instance is available to handle requests. To run this health check type, you must turn it on for your Auto Scaling group. |
evidence.table_header: | Health check type | What it checks |

claim: The VPC Lattice health check type checks whether VPC Lattice reports the instance as healthy; like the ELB check, you must turn it on for the group.
question: Is the VPC Lattice health check on by default for an Auto Scaling group?

evidence.quote: | VPC Lattice health checks | +  Checks whether VPC Lattice reports the instance as healthy, confirming whether the instance is available to handle requests. To run this health check type, you must turn it on for your Auto Scaling group. |
evidence.table_header: | Health check type | What it checks |

claim: The Amazon EBS health check type checks whether EBS volumes are reachable and pass I/O status checks; you must turn it on for the group.
question: How does an Auto Scaling group detect instances with impaired EBS volumes?

evidence.quote: | Amazon EBS health checks | +  Checks whether EBS volumes are reachable and passing I/O status checks. To run this health check type, you must turn it on for your Auto Scaling group. |
evidence.table_header: | Health check type | What it checks |

claim: If EC2 Auto Scaling detects that an instance is no longer in the running state, it treats this as an immediate failure, marks the instance Unhealthy at once and replaces it.
question: How fast does Auto Scaling act when an instance leaves the running state?

evidence.quote: However, if Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling detects that an instance is no longer in the `running` state, this situation is treated as an immediate failure. In this case, it immediately marks the instance as `Unhealthy` and replaces it.

claim: An instance affected by an EC2 scheduled event is considered unhealthy and replaced; it does not start shutting down until the time in the event timestamp.
question: What does Auto Scaling do with an instance that has an EC2 scheduled event?

values.display: considers the instance to be unhealthy

evidence.quote: If one of your instances is affected by a scheduled event, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling considers the instance to be unhealthy and replaces it. The instance doesn't start shutting down until the date and time that's specified in the timestamp is reached.

claim: Once ELB health checks are turned on for the group, an instance that Elastic Load Balancing reports as Unhealthy is marked Unhealthy at the next periodic health check and replaced.
question: After ELB health checks are turned on, what happens to an instance the load balancer reports unhealthy?

values.display: on its next periodic health check

evidence.quote: After you turn on these health checks for your Auto Scaling group, when Elastic Load Balancing reports a registered instance as `Unhealthy`, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling marks the instance `Unhealthy` on its next periodic health check and replaces it.

claim: With connection draining (deregistration delay) on the load balancer, EC2 Auto Scaling waits for in-flight requests to complete or the maximum timeout to expire before it terminates unhealthy instances.
question: Does Auto Scaling wait for in-flight requests before it terminates an unhealthy instance behind a load balancer?

values.display: waits for either in-flight requests to complete

evidence.quote: If connection draining (deregistration delay) is enabled for your load balancer, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling waits for either in-flight requests to complete or the maximum timeout to expire before it terminates unhealthy instances.

claim: The EC2 status checks and scheduled events cannot be removed from a group's health checks; to stop replacements, AWS recommends suspending the ReplaceUnhealthy and HealthCheck processes.
question: Can you turn off the EC2 status checks of an Auto Scaling group?

values.display: does not provide a way of removing the Amazon EC2 status checks

evidence.quote: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling does not provide a way of removing the Amazon EC2 status checks and scheduled events from its health checks. If you do not want instances to be replaced, we recommend that you suspend the `ReplaceUnhealthy` and `HealthCheck` process for individual Auto Scaling groups.

claim: When an instance is terminated, its EBS volumes are detached (or deleted, depending on DeleteOnTermination) and are not attached to the replacement; you attach them yourself or with a lifecycle hook.
question: Does a replacement instance get the EBS volumes of the instance it replaces?

evidence.quote: Similarly, when your instance is terminated, its attached EBS volumes are detached (or deleted depending on the volume's `DeleteOnTermination` attribute). You must manually attach these EBS volumes to the new instance, or do it automatically with a lifecycle hook-based solution.

claim: When an InService instance is unhealthy, EC2 Auto Scaling replaces it to keep the desired capacity, and the new instance launches with the group's current settings and its current launch template or launch configuration.
question: Which configuration does a replacement for an unhealthy instance use?

values.display: current settings of the Auto Scaling group
replaces it with a new instance

evidence.quote: When Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling determines that an `InService` instance is unhealthy, it replaces it with a new instance to maintain the desired capacity of the group. The new instance launches using the current settings of the Auto Scaling group and its associated launch template or launch configuration.

claim: Every instance in a group starts with a Healthy status and is assumed healthy unless EC2 Auto Scaling receives a notification that it is unhealthy.
question: What health status does a new instance in an Auto Scaling group start with?

values.display: Instances are assumed to be healthy

evidence.quote: All instances in an Auto Scaling group start with a `Healthy` status. Instances are assumed to be healthy unless Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling receives notification that they are unhealthy.

claim: EC2 Auto Scaling checks a new instance with the built-in EC2 status checks, and only after a grace period with the optional health checks enabled for the group.
question: When do the optional health checks (such as ELB) start for a new instance?

values.display: any optional health checks that you enabled

evidence.quote: Then, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling performs health checks on the instance by using the built-in Amazon EC2 status checks, and after a grace period, any optional health checks that you enabled for the group.

claim: When an instance terminates unexpectedly, for example from a Spot interruption or a manual termination, EC2 Auto Scaling launches a replacement to keep the desired capacity.
question: Does Auto Scaling replace an instance that someone terminated by hand?

evidence.quote: Unhealthy instances can also occur when an instance terminates unexpectedly, such as from a Spot Instance interruption or manual termination by a user. Again, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling will automatically launch a replacement instance in these cases to maintain the desired capacity.

claim: By default EC2 Auto Scaling ignores the results of VPC Lattice health checks; you can turn them on for the group.
question: Does an Auto Scaling group act on VPC Lattice health checks by default?

values.display: ignores the results of the VPC Lattice

evidence.quote: By default, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling ignores the results of the VPC Lattice health checks. You can optionally turn on these health checks for your Auto Scaling group.

claim: By default, new instances are provisioned at the same time as unhealthy existing instances are terminated, which might stop new requests being accepted until the new instances are fully operational.
question: By default, does Auto Scaling launch a replacement before it terminates an unhealthy instance?

values.display: new instances are provisioned at the same time

evidence.quote: By default, new instances are provisioned at the same time your existing instances are terminated, which might prevent new requests from being accepted until the new instances are fully operational.
